title: main.tsx mutates deps after construction; module-level cachedPackageId
description: main.tsx builds the AppDeps object, then on lines 64-69 reaches back into it, captures the original loadManifest in `_origLoadManifest`, and reassigns `deps.loadManifest` to a wrapper that side-effects a module-level `let cachedPackageId`. fetchPoolStats (line 47-59) then closes over that mutable. So the contract is: `fetchPoolStats(descriptor)` produces correct stats only if `loadManifest()` has resolved at least once before it is called. Nothing in the type system enforces that ordering; nothing in the code asserts on it. If the App ever calls fetchPoolStats before loadManifest (e.g. a future refactor that pre-warms a card, or tests that skip the manifest load), it silently fetches against `packageId=''`, yielding zero events from `suix_queryEvents` (no thrown error, no warning).
impact: The wiring works only by convention of the current App.tsx effect order. The intended composition (manifest → packageId → per-pool fetch) is encoded as imperative state mutation rather than data flow. A reader has to understand that `cachedPackageId` is implicit shared state to follow the data path. Reassigning a property on the deps object the App will receive is a React-foreign idiom and an antipattern in dependency-injected systems where deps are supposed to be a read-only contract.
recommendation: Load the manifest once at module top-level (outside the AppDeps object), then build deps with both loadManifest and fetchPoolStats closing over the same already-loaded LoadedManifest. e.g. `const manifestPromise = (async () => parseManifest(await (await fetch(MANIFEST_URL)).json(), MANIFEST_URL))(); const deps: AppDeps = { loadManifest: () => manifestPromise, fetchPoolStats: async (d) => fetchSinglePoolStats(RPC_URL, (await manifestPromise).deepbookPackageId, d, Date.now()) };`. No mutation, no module-level let, the dependency is a cached promise.

title: dataLayer.ts imports PoolCardData from a UI component file
description: The H-10 fix moved chain-shape types into types.ts, but PoolCardData (the UI's render contract) was left in `components/PoolCard.tsx`. dataLayer.ts and main.tsx now both import PoolCardData from the components path, inverting the natural dependency direction: the data layer depends on a UI component file. types.ts even claims in its own header comment to be the home of `UI aggregate types (PoolCardData)` — but PoolCardData is not declared there. The single-source-of-truth fix is half-applied.
impact: If anyone ever moves PoolCard or splits it into sub-components, the data layer breaks. The architecture diagram is fuzzy: a 'data layer' that imports from 'components/' is structurally the same shape as a circular dependency, just with the cycle broken by accident of which file is loaded first. The test suite cannot detect this drift because every consumer happens to import via the same path.
recommendation: Move PoolCardData and SparklinePoint declarations to types.ts (which already documents itself as their home) and have PoolCard.tsx import them as `import type { PoolCardData, SparklinePoint } from '../types.js'`. Then dataLayer.ts imports PoolCardData from types.ts and the dependency direction matches the conceptual layering.

title: FillRecord and RawFillEvent identical but declared in two modules
description: fillAggregator.ts declares `FillRecord = { poolId; timestampMs; baseQuantity; price }`. fillFetcher.ts declares `RawFillEvent` with the exact same four fields. dataLayer.ts has to manually map one to the other (lines 349-354) — a no-op rename — because TypeScript will not allow the two structurally identical types to flow without a redeclaration ceremony. This is the same drift hazard that the H-10 fix was supposed to eliminate for chain types; it survived for fill types because the consolidator only fingerprinted the manifest/order types.
impact: Three places to update if a fifth field is ever needed (the producer, the consumer, the no-op map). The map function in dataLayer.ts is dead weight that would silently swallow any future field divergence: if RawFillEvent gains a `side` field, FillRecord won't; the map will lose it. Documentation also drifts — types.ts comments mention `RawFillEntry` but neither RawFillEvent nor FillRecord is in types.ts.
recommendation: Move one canonical FillRecord (or RawFillEvent — pick one name) into types.ts. fillFetcher and fillAggregator both import it. dataLayer.ts can drop the no-op `.map(f => ({...}))` and pass rawFills directly to aggregateFills. Three modules align on one shape.

title: resolvePoolInnerFields conflates four shape variants with implicit fallbacks
description: resolvePoolInnerFields handles: (1) the T-014 fixture shape where the object directly has a `book` field; (2) the real Pool wrapper shape with `inner.fields.id.id` pointing at a Versioned; (3) a degraded case where `inner` exists but has no versionedId (returns the wrapper fields raw — pretending they are PoolInner); (4) a case where the dynamic-fields response is empty (also returns wrapper fields). Each fallback returns a different sub-shape but the function signature lies that they are all `Record<string, unknown> | null`. buildPoolInnerState then has to defensively `(field?.fields ?? field)` everywhere because it cannot tell which variant it received. The 'fixture vs production' branching is the most concerning: the production code path is choosing its behavior based on whether the response looks like a unit-test fixture. That couples the data layer to the test fixture shape — the very tautology the iter-1 review flagged elsewhere.
impact: Any future change to one of the four shapes will silently start returning a different shape variant. There is no logging to tell you which path was taken. A reader cannot answer 'what does resolvePoolInnerFields return for a real sandbox call?' without running it. The fixture-aware branch (`if 'book' in fields return fields`) makes the production code-path implicitly weaker — when the real chain returns an unexpected shape it can match the fixture branch by accident and skip the Versioned traversal.
recommendation: Split into two functions with crisp contracts: `resolvePoolInnerFromVersioned(rpcUrl, poolId): Promise<PoolInnerFields>` (the production path; throws if the Versioned/dynamic-field traversal does not yield a PoolInner) and `resolvePoolInnerFromDirect(obj): PoolInnerFields | null` (the fixture/direct path). Have buildPoolInnerState branch explicitly. Or, better: change the T-014 fixture to return the realistic Pool wrapper shape and delete the fixture branch entirely; the production code path then has one variant.

title: Order.price? injection unimplemented; CR-2 fix is a comment, not code
description: The CR-2 fix added an optional `price?: number` to Order so the data layer can inject the OrderInfo event price and computeMarketStats can prefer it. This works around the fact that decodeBidPrice gives the wrong answer on real chain order_ids. But: (a) the data layer in dataLayer.ts.traverseBigVector (lines 196-210) never actually populates `price` — the field is constructed from `orderFields['order_id']`, `quantity`, `filled_quantity`, `status` only; (b) the comment on line 53-54 of marketStats.ts says `For bids, the order_id decode is tautologically correct against test fixtures but wrong against real chain order_ids. Prefer injected price.` admitting in a code comment that the production path will use the wrong path because nothing injects the right one. So the iter-1 CR-2 verdict (`bid prices wrong by orders of magnitude on every live pool`) is structurally not fixed — the data layer never invokes the OrderInfo→Order join the design supposedly enables.
impact: The Order.price field is documented infrastructure for a fix that was not implemented. computeMarketStats now has two branches but the second branch is dead in production. The cycle ships a comment promising correctness without a code path that delivers it. AC1.4's `bestBid <= mid <= bestAsk` invariant remains unsatisfiable on live data; the iter-1 critical was downgraded by means of a TODO disguised as a fix.
recommendation: Either (a) actually wire the OrderInfo→Order join in dataLayer.ts (the queryEventsFn already collects price per fill on lines 281-284, so the building blocks exist; cross-reference orders by their `order_id` against a map of OrderInfo events to populate Order.price); or (b) re-derive the bid encoding empirically from the captured chain-shape sample (`order_id: 12377783720203182843884075`, `price: 671000`) and fix decodeBidPrice itself. Path (a) was the documented preference; either way, do not ship an optional field that nothing populates.

title: App.tsx polling effect duplicates entire fetch+map block from initial-load
description: The initial-load effect (lines 41-87) and the polling effect (lines 91-125) duplicate ~30 lines: same `Promise.allSettled(pools.map(deps.fetchPoolStats))`, same sentinel-card-on-rejection construction, same poolErrors aggregation, same setState shape. The only divergence is the initial-load path also calls deps.loadManifest first. If the sentinel card shape ever changes, two places must update. If the error-message extraction logic changes, two places. If a third call site (manual refresh button, first-render race recovery) is added, three places.
impact: Two effects, two re-implementations of the same pipeline, no shared helper. Maintenance hazard. Also makes the polling effect non-cancellable — the original initial-load effect tracks a `cancelled` flag, the polling effect does not, so a setState fires on an unmounted component if the interval's last batch resolves after unmount. (React 19 will warn but not error.)
recommendation: Extract `async function refreshAll(deps, pools): Promise<{ cards, poolErrors }>` and have both effects call it. Then the polling effect is `setInterval(() => refreshAll(deps, pools).then(({cards, poolErrors}) => { if (!cancelled) setState({status:'ready', cards, poolErrors}) }), 20_000)` with its own cancelled flag.

title: Polling effect setState fires after unmount; missing cancelled flag
description: The polling effect's setInterval callback (lines 94-122) is `async` and calls setState (line 121) after awaiting Promise.allSettled. The cleanup function only calls `clearInterval(intervalId)` — it does not flip a `cancelled` flag the async callback could check before setState. So if the component unmounts after an interval tick has fired but before its allSettled resolves, the setState lands on an unmounted component. (Compare with the initial-load effect on lines 41-87, which correctly uses a `cancelled` flag.) This is a classic React useEffect pitfall.
impact: React 19 warns rather than errors on stale-state updates, but the symptom is real: in test or HMR scenarios where the App mounts and unmounts repeatedly, polling effects from previous mounts may stomp on the new mount's state. With a 20 s interval and short mount lifecycle (e.g. story navigation, route changes if Slot 1 ever expands), this becomes a real bug.
recommendation: Add the same `let cancelled = false` pattern as the initial-load effect. Inside the setInterval callback, after await, check `if (!cancelled) setState(...)`. The cleanup sets `cancelled = true` and clears the interval. Or migrate the polling to use AbortController and pass signal through to deps.fetchPoolStats so in-flight RPC calls are cancelled too.

title: vite.config.ts middleware hard-codes home-relative manifest path
description: vite.config.ts hard-codes the manifest path as `homedir() / workspace / deepbook-sandbox / sandbox / deployments / localnet.json`. The middleware logic — file IO, content-type, error message — sits inline in `configureServer`. Two design concerns: (a) the path coupling assumes a specific workspace layout (`~/workspace/deepbook-sandbox/`) that is not documented anywhere outside this file; a developer using a different checkout location has to edit vite.config.ts. The contract section 'Integration / sandbox contract' explicitly said this choice should be configurable per-environment. (b) Filesystem-IO middleware in vite.config.ts is fine for a one-off, but as soon as Slot 2 or 3 needs the same manifest, this logic gets copy-pasted into another vite.config — a small Vite plugin (`pluginManifestProxy()`) would let it be shared.
impact: Friction for any developer whose sandbox checkout is not at exactly `~/workspace/deepbook-sandbox/`. The error response (line 39-40) at least surfaces the path so the failure is debuggable, which mitigates severity. But the current architecture leaks a setup assumption into a build-config file rather than a documented env var or config block.
recommendation: Read the path from an env var with the current default: `const MANIFEST_DISK_PATH = process.env.SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH ?? path.join(homedir(), 'workspace', 'deepbook-sandbox', 'sandbox', 'deployments', 'localnet.json')`. Mention `SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH` in the README/runbook. Optionally extract to `vite-plugin-sandbox-manifest.ts` for reuse by Slot 2/3 (but this is optional — current scope is only Slot 1).

title: rpcId module-level mutable counter persists; iter-1 R2-010 unfixed
description: Iter-1 R2-010 flagged `let rpcId = 0;` at module scope as a small global-state hazard. The iter-2 rewrite of dataLayer.ts kept it (line 43). It is still inert today (JSON-RPC ids only need uniqueness within a connection, and no test asserts on the id), but it remains a global-state design footgun: any future test that asserts on the id will be order-dependent on test execution because the counter persists across imports.
impact: Negligible at runtime. The 'rest of the codebase consciously injects state via args' observation from iter-1 still applies — App takes deps, runDataLayer takes manifest+rpcUrl, only this counter is stowaway state. Slightly harder to reason about than necessary.
recommendation: Move the counter into a closure created per `runDataLayer` invocation (or per-rpc-client factory), or use `crypto.randomUUID()` / `Date.now()` for the id. Either way, drop the module-level mutable.

title: manifest.ts re-exports types from types.ts; two canonical paths
description: manifest.ts on lines 22-23 does both `export type { PoolDescriptor, LoadedManifest } from './types.js';` and `import type { LoadedManifest, PoolDescriptor } from './types.js';`. The re-export exists to support consumers that import these types from manifest.ts (e.g. App.tsx line 14, dataLayer.ts line 19). Now that types.ts is the documented source of truth, the re-export adds a second canonical path for the same types without any value — the consolidator can no longer tell which file is canonical for these types just by reading imports.
impact: Doubles the surface area for type drift: a future change that adds a field to LoadedManifest in types.ts will silently propagate, but a future change that wraps LoadedManifest in manifest.ts (e.g. branding) will diverge from types.ts. Also confuses future readers about whether manifest.ts owns these types or just consumes them.
recommendation: Drop the re-export from manifest.ts. Update App.tsx (line 14) and dataLayer.ts (line 19) to `import type { ... } from './types.js'` directly. One canonical home for the types, every consumer imports from it.
evidence:
export type { PoolDescriptor, LoadedManifest } from './types.js';
import type { LoadedManifest, PoolDescriptor } from './types.js';

title: fetchSinglePoolStats exported as alias of fetchPoolStats; two names
description: dataLayer.ts declares `async function fetchPoolStats(...)` (line 324) and at the bottom (line 413) does `export { fetchPoolStats as fetchSinglePoolStats }`. main.tsx (line 24, 58) imports it as fetchSinglePoolStats. Inside dataLayer.ts (line 394) runDataLayer calls the same function via the original name. Two names for one function, with no explanation in comments. The 'public name' (fetchSinglePoolStats) and the 'internal name' (fetchPoolStats) suggest a deliberate public-vs-private distinction, but both are in the same module and both are exported.
impact: Reader friction: anyone tracing 'where is fetchSinglePoolStats defined' has to grep for both names. Search-and-replace tooling will miss one of the two. Tests that want to mock the function have to know to mock fetchPoolStats internally but fetchSinglePoolStats externally.
recommendation: Pick one name. If the public name is fetchSinglePoolStats, rename the internal function and update line 394's caller; drop the alias export. If the public name is fetchPoolStats, update main.tsx imports. The naming should reflect the function's job — `fetchPoolStats` is fine because the 'single' modifier is implicit in the lack of a plural.
